solutions.check: 30 entries verified against the grid (lengths, crossings, linked-clue mapping)

clue.text: Hacks, maybe from Sun, Cameron's prime piss-takers, trap LibDem leader

indicators.note: to trap something is to hold it inside, so the mockers enclose the party leader

parts.note: S is the standard abbreviation for Sun (Sunday, or the star)

indicators.note: the prime part of something is its foremost portion, so only the opening letter of the name is kept

parts.note: first letter of the Prime Minister's name
ribbers are people who tease or mock

indicators.note: a leader goes in front, so just the initial letter of the party name counts

parts.note: first letter of the party's name

explanation.surface: Tabloid journalists from the Sun, David Cameron's leading mockers, set out to ambush the Liberal Democrat leader.
explanation.walkthrough: The Sun is the British tabloid, but here it is just S; the hacks of the definition are newspaper writers in general.
explanation.definitionFit: Scribblers is a disparaging term for writers, especially jobbing journalists, which is what hacks are.

clue.text: Military unit: "nothing fits in pisspoor torch!"

indicators.note: something that fits in goes inside, so the zero is slotted into the other letters
something pisspoor is badly made, so the letters of the following word are in a botched order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged
nothing is zero, written O

explanation.surface: A soldier complains that nothing fits inside his useless torch.
explanation.walkthrough: Torch is rearranged to C-HORT and the O of nothing goes in after the C.
explanation.definitionFit: A cohort was a tenth of a Roman legion, a body of several hundred soldiers.

clue.text: It's grim dancing with anus ring, idiot!

indicators.note: letters that are dancing are moving around and changing places

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
a ring is round, the shape of the letter O

explanation.surface: A crude playground insult about some unpleasant dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: Ring supplies an O before the shuffle; grim and anus give the other eight letters.
explanation.definitionFit: An ignoramus is an ignorant, stupid person, a fair synonym for an idiot.

clue.text: "Balls gone!" over-the-top luvvie said after a sneeze?

indicators.note: we are to hear the phrase as a theatrical, affected speaker would pronounce it, clipping the vowel

parts.note: having no balls is being ball-less, which a gushing thespian swallows to one syllable

explanation.surface: A camp actor squeals that he has been castrated, or simply blesses someone who sneezed.
explanation.walkthrough: A loose sound-alike typical of this setter: ball-less, run together in a luvvie's drawl, comes out close to the one-word blessing.
explanation.definitionFit: "Bless you" is the customary response to a sneeze, often shortened to the single word.

clue.text: (& 22dn.) Yesmen 'yo' a dodgy fatcat's bonus, say

indicators.note: something dodgy is unreliable and crooked, so the letters are not in their honest order

parts.note: the letters of the three words together

explanation.surface: Sycophants greet the shady payout to a rich executive.
explanation.definitionFit: A fat-cat's bonus is an example of money obtained with little effort, hence the 'say'.

clue.text: It's used to scour LibDem peer, then make love at length

parts.note: David Steel, former Liberal leader, now Lord Steel
to make love in the old sense is to court, to woo
L is the standard abbreviation for length

explanation.surface: A Liberal Democrat lord cleans up, then has a long romantic session.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Make love' is meant in its old courting sense; David Steel led the Liberal Party and sits in the Lords.
explanation.definitionFit: Steel wool is an abrasive pad of fine metal fibres for scrubbing pans clean.

clue.text: Country copper has testicles reduced by 60%

indicators.note: cutting by sixty per cent leaves two fifths, so three of five letters are removed

parts.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
balls is slang for testicles

explanation.surface: A policeman with shrunken testicles, the copper of the clue being a cop.
explanation.walkthrough: Copper is the chemical element, not a policeman; of the five letters of balls only the first two remain.
explanation.definitionFit: Cuba is an island nation in the Caribbean.

clue.text: Whip takes Miliband back, as one not yet ready for command?

definitions.text: one not yet ready for command?

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it, so the lash encloses the name

parts.note: a cat o' nine tails is a whip

indicators.note: going back means reading from the end, so the first name is turned round

parts.note: Ed Miliband, then Labour leader

explanation.surface: A party whip lets Ed Miliband back in, though he is not yet fit to lead.
explanation.walkthrough: Whip looks like the party official but is the cat o' nine tails; Ed, read backwards, sits inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A cadet is a trainee officer, someone still learning before being given command.

clue.text: Boozers, home to cold, unprofessional, sullied bankers

indicators.note: a place that is home to things houses them, so the drinking places hold what follows

parts.note: boozers are pubs, places with bars
C is the abbreviation for cold, as on taps
lay means not belonging to a profession, as in a layman

explanation.surface: Pubs where cold, amateurish, disgraced financiers drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Boozers is British slang for pubs. The 2012 Libor-rigging scandal had just tainted Barclays, hence sullied.
explanation.definitionFit: Barclays is a major British bank whose reputation was damaged by the Libor scandal of 2012.

clue.text: (& 19/27) Perhaps Met. officers' hint about pornographic bit of verse

indicators.note: about can mean around or out of order, so these letters are moved round

parts.note: the four letters rearranged
a blue film is pornographic
a line is one part of a poem

explanation.surface: Police drop hints about an obscene poem.
explanation.walkthrough: The Met is London's Metropolitan Police; blue for smutty is everyday British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: The thin blue line is a nickname for the police, seen as the barrier between order and chaos; Met officers are an example.

clue.text: Soap arse during festivals

indicators.note: something happening during an event lies within it, so one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: Easter is a spring festival, here pluralised
the rear end

explanation.surface: Someone dropping the soap while at a festival.
explanation.walkthrough: EastEnders is the long-running BBC soap opera set in London's East End.
explanation.definitionFit: EastEnders is a British television soap opera, so it is an example of a soap.

clue.text: Member support produces resistance in master nuts

indicators.note: the wordplay produces its letter in the middle, with in showing where it goes
something nuts is crazy, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: letters of master rearranged
R is the symbol for electrical resistance

explanation.surface: A crude remark about genitals, with member and nuts both doing smutty work.
explanation.walkthrough: Member means a limb, the arm; the R slips into the scrambled master after ARM.
explanation.definitionFit: An armrest supports the arm, and an arm is a member in the sense of a limb.

clue.text: A "doll" screwed officer inside — nothing omitted

indicators.note: screwed means twisted or wrecked, so the letters are distorted
inside places one piece within the other

parts.note: the letters of a and doll rearranged
Lt is the abbreviation for lieutenant

explanation.surface: An officer has been bedding a woman, and the full story is out.
explanation.walkthrough: Screwed is sexual in the surface but signals the letter shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: All told means in total, counting everything, so with nothing left out.

clue.text: (& 15ac.) Candidate needing hand, right, with suspect money?

indicators.note: something suspect is not straight, so the letters are not in honest order

parts.note: mitt is slang for a hand
R is short for right
letters of money rearranged

explanation.surface: A politician needs a hand from the right wing and some questionable funding.
explanation.walkthrough: In 2012 Romney was the Republican presidential candidate, a wealthy man whose money drew scrutiny.
explanation.definitionFit: Mitt Romney was the Republican nominee in the 2012 US presidential election.

clue.text: Go beyond rants about Conservative demise

indicators.note: about can mean around or out of order, so these letters are moved round

parts.note: the letters rearranged
C is the abbreviation for Conservative
a demise is an end

explanation.surface: A commentator's tirades about the fall of the Tories go too far.
explanation.definitionFit: To transcend is to rise above or exceed the limits of something.

clue.text: see 13ac.
Liberal feud hosted by twit, of necessity

indicators.note: a guest hosted by someone is inside their home, so the first group goes within the second

parts.note: a nelly is a silly person, as in 'not on your nelly'

indicators.note: liberal means free and unrestrained, so the letters are let loose from their order

parts.note: taken as written, to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A Liberal quarrel is put up with by a fool, because it has to be.
explanation.walkthrough: Liberal looks like the party, abbreviated L, but it means free and unrestrained; the reworked feud sits after the first two letters of NELLY.
explanation.definitionFit: Needfully is an old adverb meaning necessarily, unavoidably.

clue.text: Uppermost in a Tory hogging constant repeated phrase

indicators.note: to hog something is to keep it to oneself, so the words hold the solution concealed within them

parts.note: the letters run across the end of the first word and into the last

explanation.surface: A senior Conservative monopolises a fixed refrain.
explanation.walkthrough: Uppermost looks like a letter-position instruction; it simply holds the start of the run of letters.
explanation.definitionFit: In music an ostinato is a motif or phrase persistently repeated, from the Italian for obstinate.

clue.text: Band, one with ultimately cheesy Jagger-style move?

parts.note: a sash is a band of cloth
one is the indefinite article a

indicators.note: ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of the word is used

parts.note: last letter of the word

explanation.surface: A rock group and one cheesy singer strutting like Mick Jagger.
explanation.walkthrough: Band suggests a group like the Rolling Stones but is the strip of cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: To sashay is to walk with an exaggerated swing of the hips, as Jagger famously does on stage.

clue.text: see 9ac.
Gold medallist as a pain-in-the-arse car insurance plugger?

definitions.meaning: second meaning: film director Michael ..., who fronted irritating esure TV adverts

explanation.walkthrough: Michael Winner, film director, appeared in UK adverts for esure car insurance with the catchphrase 'Calm down, dear'.
explanation.definitionFit: A gold medallist is the victor of an event; the surname also identifies the director who advertised insurance.

clue.text: Vicious about young female's discharge

indicators.note: turned about means facing the other way, so the name is written backwards

parts.note: Sid Vicious, bassist of the Sex Pistols
a miss is a girl

explanation.surface: A comment on a spiteful girl's vaginal discharge, in Private Eye's smutty manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Vicious is not an adjective here but the stage surname of punk musician Sid Vicious.
explanation.definitionFit: To discharge someone from a job or the army is to dismiss them.

clue.text: see 5dn.
Beer + comedian = twat

parts.note: a half is a half-pint of beer
a wit is a funny person

explanation.surface: An equation: a drinking comic adds up to an idiot.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordering 'a half' in a British pub means half a pint of beer.
explanation.definitionFit: Twat is British slang for a stupid person, which is what a halfwit is.

clue.text: Hassle from rag — go berserk

indicators.note: going berserk is running wild, so the letters are thrown into disorder

parts.note: the letters of both words together

explanation.surface: A newspaper, the rag, goes wild and causes trouble.
explanation.definitionFit: Aggro is British slang for aggravation, trouble or aggressive bother.

clue.text: see 28ac.
Doing a banker and cleaning up?

definitions.meaning: first meaning: passing dirty money through the financial system, as some banks were found to do

explanation.walkthrough: Doing a banker sounds like a crime caper; banks such as HSBC were fined in 2012 for processing criminal money.
explanation.definitionFit: The word covers both washing and ironing clothes and disguising the origin of illegally obtained funds.

clue.text: see 9ac.
(& 25dn.) Band on end of tiny penis? That's novel

parts.note: a mob is a gang, a band of people

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last character, so only that is kept

parts.note: last letter of the word
slang

explanation.surface: A schoolboy joke about a small penis, ending with 'that's new'.
explanation.walkthrough: That's novel reads as 'that's new', but novel is the noun: a book.
explanation.definitionFit: Moby-Dick is Herman Melville's 1851 novel about the hunt for a white whale.

clue.text: Royal who had lots of men "mounting" and "going down"

definitions.text: Royal who had lots of men "mounting" and "going down"

parts.words: Royal who had lots of men "mounting" and "going down"
parts.note: surface reading: a lurid rumour about a royal's sex life
setter's reading: the nursery rhyme noble who had ten thousand men and marched them up to the top of the hill and down again

explanation.walkthrough: The quoted words are sexual in the surface but describe marching uphill and back down in the nursery rhyme; the title was also Prince Andrew's.
explanation.definitionFit: The Grand Old Duke of York in the nursery rhyme commanded ten thousand men, a royal title held by Prince Andrew.
